Fields and degrees in stem are very specific. In my university (ignoring a few legitimately duplicate programs that are taught more lab based vs more theory), we have, to name a few off the top of my head: electrical engineering, microelectronics engineering, computer engineering, computer science, computing and information technologies, electronic and telecommunications technology, network and systems engineering, applied informatics. Quite a list (and I'm ignoring a number of high level specific degrees like software engineering, cyber security, game design). All of those degree programs deal specifically with the design or implementation of computers or electronics, or systems relying on them, and most of them do so in the context of hardware to an extent (with the primary exception of computer science). Some of those degrees have "engineering" in them, others do not. That may seem trivial, but the accreditation agencies for colleges enforce certain requirements for an "engineering" degree, which is different than the requirements for a degree that says "science," even though the general degree title is still a bachelors of science. An "electronics degree" (the exact phrase used by the person in the article to describe his degree), is most likely to be equivalent in content area and graduation requirements to electronics and telecommunications technology. Not electrical engineering. Not only are the academic requirements different, the content areas are completely different. EE focuses on design, whereas ETT (or electronics) is going to focus on examining existing standards and deciding when to use them to say, implement a network expansion for a major telco. Electrical engineers couldn't do that, because they don't cover it. ETT can't do design, because they haven't been trained in it. In fact ETT is far closer to network and systems administration than it is to electrical eng, comp eng, or micro-e. Its also closer to that applied informatics degree than it is to electrical engineering. Just because it has similar words in the name does NOT make it a similar degree in what it covers or in its academic rigor.
